I worry about A scoring method that has subjective elements. So I like a static model where it's harder to play games. with the forecast in terms of the revenue consequence of what you're trying to achieve. Without question, there are dynamic impacts to tax cut legislation. Growth is accelerated. Maybe growth is slowed down. It depends on how you structure your taxes. Should that be reflected in a scoring? You certainly make an academic case for it. The more theoretical things become in terms of trying to understand the budget impact of the tax cut, the more the gains can be played in terms of not fully accounting for the revenue loss in a long-term budget projection. Last weekend I heard an extremely conservative House Republican indicate that they were ready to move on to tax reform and It wouldn't have to all be paid for because There was going to be growth created by the tax cut. I think there will be growth created by tax cuts, at least in the near term. But if you start down the road of dynamic scoring, and there will be dynamic scoring in the tax reform debate ahead, it can really be abused in terms of fiction.
